papers.title: Universal Jaynes-Cummings Control of an Oscillator
papers.abstract: The Jaynes-Cummings (JC) interaction-the coherent exchange of excitations between a two-level system and a harmonic oscillator-is one of the fundamental interactions of quantum optics, realized across platforms such as cavity quantum electrodynamics, trapped ions, mechanical resonators, and superconducting circuits. Although JC interactions and qubit rotations form a universal gate set for oscillator control, practical implementations have not been demonstrated. Here we develop and experimentally demonstrate universal JC-based oscillator control by compiling arbitrary unitary gates into sequences of JC interactions and qubit rotations. In our experiment, the oscillator is realized using a mode of a high quality factor microwave cavity and the ancilla qubit using a superconducting transmon circuit, with the JC interaction implemented by a sideband interaction enabled by the Josephson nonlinearity. The native gates are constructed to be closed below a chosen cutoff photon number, encoding a qudit with suppressed leakage errors, while ancilla relaxation errors are detectable. We further find that the dispersive shift serves as a compilation resource that reduces circuit depths. We demonstrate universal qudit control and implement a single-qutrit gate set with a mean post-selected process fidelity of 96.3%, as well as ququart and ququint shift gates. These results establish Jaynes-Cummings control as a practical route to universal oscillator control, enabling programmable bosonic processors across a variety of quantum platforms.

similar_to.title: A mid-circuit erasure check on a dual-rail cavity qubit using the joint-photon number-splitting regime of circuit QED

summary.summary: This work demonstrates universal control of a superconducting cavity mode using Jaynes-Cummings (JC) interactions between the cavity and a transmon ancilla, achieving a mean post-selected process fidelity of 96.3% for qutrit gates with leakage errors suppressed by construction. The JC interaction is realized via sideband drives on the transmon, and the dispersive shift is exploited as a compilation resource to reduce circuit depth from $\mathcal{O}(d^2)$ layers without detuning optimization to lower effective depths for high-dimensional qudits.
summary.motivation: Dispersive-shift-based approaches for oscillator control suffer from ancilla-mediated errors that limit fidelity, especially as cavity coherence times improve beyond milliseconds. JC-based control promises leakage suppression and relaxation-error detectability, but practical implementations of universal control have been lacking.
summary.method: Arbitrary qudit unitaries are compiled into sequences of ancilla rotations between transmon $|g\rangle$ and $|f\rangle$ states and JC rotations that perform $2\pi$ operations on the $|f, d-1\rangle \leftrightarrow |g, d\rangle$ transition. The JC detuning $\delta$ is treated as an optimization parameter to enhance mixing across Fock manifolds and reduce circuit depth; sideband drives with programmable phase and frequency chirps implement the JC interaction with $g_{\mathrm{JC}}/2\pi \approx 100$ kHz and $|\chi_f/g_{\mathrm{JC}}| \approx 0.5$ in the experimental device.
summary.result: A complete qutrit universal gate set (Clifford generators $H$, $S$ and non-Clifford $T$ gate) is demonstrated with post-selected process fidelities of 95.7% rising to 96.3% with global phase correction; ququart and ququint shift gates reach 95.3% and 94.2% fidelity respectively. Circuit depth scales as $\mathcal{O}(d^2)$ and gate time as $\mathcal{O}(d^{3/2})$ due to photon-number-dependent JC rate enhancement.

papers.title: Measurement and Control of the Complex Berry Phase in a Quantum System
papers.abstract: The Berry phase is a geometric phase acquired during adiabatic evolution over a closed loop in parameter space. It plays an essential role in geometric quantum gates and other phase-based protocols. In non-Hermitian systems, the Berry phase is complex, introducing fundamentally new geometric effects, including state amplification. In this work, we report experimental measurement of both the real and imaginary components of a Berry phase in a fully quantum system using a superconducting transmon circuit with engineered dissipation. We also demonstrate the path-dependent effects of the imaginary part on the dissipation and its utility in the implementation of non-unitary quantum control. These findings establish a clear geometric distinction between the real and imaginary components of the Berry phase and experimentally confirm the unique adiabatic behavior of non-Hermitian quantum systems.

similar_to.title: Measurement-induced state transitions in a superconducting qubit: Beyond the rotating wave approximation
Characterization of drive-induced unwanted state transitions in superconducting circuits

summary.summary: This work reports experimental measurement of both real and imaginary components of the Berry phase in a superconducting transmon circuit with engineered dissipation, realizing a non-Hermitian two-level system through postselection on no-jump trajectories. The imaginary Berry phase arises from state-dependent amplification or attenuation during adiabatic evolution and enables non-unitary geometric quantum control.
summary.motivation: Complex Berry phases in non-Hermitian systems exhibit fundamentally different geometric effects compared to Hermitian systems, but have only been observed in classical platforms; demonstrating control of both real and imaginary components in a quantum system would establish new capabilities for geometric phase-based protocols and non-unitary quantum operations.
summary.method: The team engineered a differential decay rate $\Gamma = 0.426$ µs$^{-1}$ between $|e\rangle$ and $|f\rangle$ states of a transmon by tuning dissipation, then measured the real geometric phase $\theta^{(r)}$ via interferometric quantum state tomography with two sequential adiabatic loops around closed paths in parameter space, and extracted the imaginary geometric phase $\theta^{(\mathrm{im})}$ from survival probability ratios under opposite loop directions.
summary.result: For $3$ MHz detuning and drive amplitude $J/2\pi \approx 1$–$5$ MHz over loops of duration $T=3$ µs, the measured real and imaginary geometric phases agreed with theoretical predictions; using the imaginary phase, non-unitary geometric gates were demonstrated that selectively amplify or attenuate eigenstate probabilities with biasing factors proportional to $e^{\pm 4\theta^{(\mathrm{im})}}$, reaching magnitudes $|\theta^{(\mathrm{im})}| \sim 0.08$–$0.17$ rad.

papers.title: Cryogenic Time-Division-Multiplexed Voltage Control for Scalable Trapped-Ion Quantum Processors
papers.abstract: Trapped-ion quantum computers based on the quantum charge-coupled device architecture require on the order of ten trap electrodes per qubit, making the number of vacuum feedthroughs a bottleneck at the system scale. Time-division multiplexed (TDM)-based voltage control for trap electrodes provides a natural route to alleviate this constraint. However, previous studies have been limited to architectural proposals for static trap-potential compensation and room-temperature demonstrations of dynamic-electrode control, leaving cryogenic operation of TDM-based voltage control for static and dynamic electrodes experimentally unexplored. In this study, we develop and cryogenically validate TDM-based voltage control schemes for two distinct electrode classes. For static electrodes used in trap-potential compensation, we implement a 32-channel demultiplexed system operating at approximately 27~K, achieving an effective voltage update rate of 37.5~kHz with an output range of $\pm10~\mathrm{V}$ per channel. For dynamic electrodes used in ion operations, such as shuttling, we implement a four-channel demultiplexed system operating at approximately 14~K, achieving an effective voltage update rate of 1~MHz with a comparable output range. These results establish TDM-based voltage control as a practical approach for both electrode classes, providing a path for mitigating the vacuum feedthrough bottleneck in scalable trapped-ion quantum processors.

similar_to.title: Superconducting Flux Memory for Cryogenic Applications
Erasure qubits: Overcoming the $T_1$ limit in superconducting circuits

summary.summary: This work demonstrates cryogenic time-division-multiplexed (TDM) voltage control for trapped-ion quantum processors, implementing a 32-channel static-electrode demultiplexer at 27 K with 37.5 kHz update rate and a four-channel dynamic-electrode demultiplexer at 14 K with 1 MHz update rate, both operating over $\pm 10$ V. The results validate TDM as a practical approach to mitigate the vacuum feedthrough bottleneck in scalable quantum-charge-coupled-device (QCCD) architectures, reducing required feedthrough connections from 32 to 8 for the static system.
summary.motivation: QCCD trapped-ion systems require approximately ten electrodes per qubit, creating a wiring bottleneck through the limited number of vacuum feedthroughs as systems approach 100+ qubits. Previous TDM proposals remained either architectural or limited to room-temperature demonstrations, leaving cryogenic operation of both static and dynamic electrode control experimentally unvalidated.
summary.method: Two prototype demultiplexed systems were developed and operated cryogenically: a static-electrode control system using cascaded 8:1 TMUX6208 switches with 2.7 nF and 470 pF holding capacitors at 27 K, and a dynamic-electrode control system using a four-channel TMUX6111 switch with 120 pF capacitors at 14 K, both fed by room-temperature DACs and FPGA-controlled logic.
summary.result: The static system achieved $37.5$ kHz per-channel update rate with measured DC output across all 32 channels; the dynamic system achieved $1$ MHz per-channel update rate and delivered time-multiplexed sinusoidal waveforms to four channels, with measured crosstalk levels of $-12$ dB (static) and $-29$ to $-35$ dB (dynamic).

papers.title: Quantum Error Correction Assisted Axion Search in CMOS Spin Qubit Arrays
papers.abstract: Searches for axion and axionlike dark matter based on solid-state spin qubits are fundamentally limited by strong longitudinal dephasing, which rapidly suppresses the sensitivity gains offered by entanglement. Here we show that quantum error correction (QEC) can substantially enhance axion search sensitivity in realistic semiconductor spin qubit platforms by mitigating this dominant noise source. By integrating an optimally chosen repetition code QEC with logical GHZ block entanglement, we derive closed-form expressions for the quantum Fisher information that explicitly incorporate the finite coherence time of the axion field. Our analysis demonstrates that modest QEC cycle frequencies are sufficient to significantly reduce the effective dephasing rate, thereby restoring a broad parameter regime in which entanglement-enhanced sensing surpasses the standard quantum limit. Projecting these results onto CMOS-compatible device parameters, we find that QEC-protected entangled sensing can revive otherwise inaccessible quantum advantages, yielding up to order-of-magnitude improvements in sensitivity to the axion-electron coupling $g_{ae}$. These results establish a practical and theoretically controlled pathway for using QEC to improve qubit array searches for physics beyond the Standard Model.

similar_to.title: Demonstrating Quantum Error Correction that Extends the Lifetime of Quantum Information
Correlated Charge Noise and Relaxation Errors in Superconducting Qubits

summary.summary: This paper demonstrates that repetition-code quantum error correction (QEC) can substantially enhance axion dark matter search sensitivity in CMOS semiconductor spin qubit arrays by mitigating longitudinal dephasing that otherwise suppresses entanglement gain. Integrating repetition codes with logical GHZ block entanglement yields closed-form quantum Fisher information expressions showing that modest QEC cycle frequencies restore multi-qubit sensing advantages across a broad axion mass range.
summary.motivation: Semiconductor spin qubit platforms searching for axion-electron coupling via entangled GHZ states suffer from strong local longitudinal dephasing ($T_2^* \sim 100$ µs in current devices with $T_{2,1/f} \sim 200$ µs), which rapidly suppresses the $\sqrt{N_\mathrm{phys}}$ sensitivity gain and makes unencoded entanglement compete only with the standard quantum limit.
summary.method: The authors combine a phase-flip repetition code (encoding each logical qubit in $n_\mathrm{rep}$ physical spins) with logical GHZ states of size $k_L$, deriving the effective logical dephasing rate $\gamma_\mathrm{eff}(n_\mathrm{rep})$ that replaces the physical rate $\gamma_\mathrm{loc}$, and optimizing the quantum Fisher information by balancing signal amplification against dephasing of the entangled state at each axion mass.
summary.result: With realistic Si/SiGe CMOS parameters ($p_g, p_m \sim 10^{-4}$, $\tau_\mathrm{cyc} = 2$ µs, $T_{2,M} = 2$ ms), an optimized configuration $(n_\mathrm{rep}, k_L) = (13, 14)$ achieves a Fisher information gain $\eta_\mathrm{seg} \approx 11.1$ relative to the SQL benchmark, yielding approximately order-of-magnitude improvement in projected sensitivity to $g_{ae}$ across the mass range $10^{-6}$–$10^{-3}$ eV where $T_\mathrm{seg}$ is hardware-limited.
